theme: Children of God; love as the test of genuine faith
readingInstruction: Read 1 John 3:1-24. John speaks of the great love of the Father, the family likeness of God’s children, and love as the test of life. Notice the contrast between the children of God and the children of the devil.
settingTheScene: In this chapter John continues his tests of genuine faith. These tests are not given to make believers anxious but to give assurance. Those who have been born of God will show a family likeness: they practice righteousness, they turn from sin, and they love their brothers and sisters. Cain is the example of the opposite. At the center is the cross as the pattern of love.
observation: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (v. 1).
“When he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (v. 2).
“The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil” (v. 8).
“No one born of God makes a practice of sinning” (v. 9).
“We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers” (v. 14).
“By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (v. 16).
“Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth” (v. 18).
“For whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (v. 20).
interpretation:
John begins with amazement: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are.” We are not just treated as children; we are children. The world does not recognize us, because it did not know him. And the future is greater: “Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.” The hope of seeing Christ and being like him is a power for holiness now.

Then comes the connection between sin and the new birth. “Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.” Christ appeared to take away sins, and in him there is no sin. “The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.” Then the verse that has puzzled many: “No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him, and he cannot keep on sinning because he has been born of God.” Taken alone it seems to teach sinless perfection, but John already said in 1:8 that anyone who claims to be without sin is a liar. The verbs in the Greek are in the present tense and describe continuous, habitual action. A child of God may sin but cannot settle into sin as a way of life, because a new nature has been planted in him. So the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest: “Whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.”

The message from the beginning: “that we should love one another.” Not like Cain, who murdered his brother because his deeds were evil. “Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.” And then: “We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.” The Christian does not love in order to receive life; love is the evidence that life has been received.

The definition of love is the cross: “By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” This leads to a very practical word: “But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him? Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.” By this, we know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him.

Then a pastoral comfort for troubled consciences: “For whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.” Some read this as comfort: even when our conscience accuses us, God knows our sincere desire to love him and is greater than our accusing heart. Others read it as a warning that God sees all. In context, comfort is the more natural meaning. The chapter ends with the twin commands: “that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another.” And the one who keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him, and “we know by this that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.”
connection: John 1:12-13 and Romans 8:14-17 speak of becoming children of God. Philippians 3:20-21 and Romans 8:29 promise we will be like Christ. Genesis 3:15 and Colossians 2:15 speak of the defeat of the devil. Genesis 4:1-12 is the story of Cain. John 5:24 says believers have passed from death to life. John 15:13 says there is no greater love than laying down one’s life. Romans 5:8 shows God’s love in Christ’s death. Matthew 25:31-46 ties judgment to care for the needy. James 2:15-17 repeats the point about love in deed. Romans 8:1 and 8:16 offer assurance for the condemning heart.
application:
Spend time with verse 1 and let it sink in: you are a child of God. Thank the Father for his lavish love.

Look for one practical way to love “in deed and in truth” this week, perhaps meeting a financial or practical need in your church.

If your heart condemns you, pray verse 20 and rest in God’s greater knowledge and mercy.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the love that makes you his child.
Ask him to teach you to love in deed and truth.
Ask him to give you assurance.
